창원시는 현재 안정적인 정수장 운영을 통해 충분한 수돗물 공급을 유지하고 있으며, 기후위기·재난 상황에도 대비한 비상 공급망 체계 구축을 적극적으로 추진하고 있습니다. 

향후 5~10년간 물 수요가 증가할 것으로 전망되나, 창원시는 시설 확충·관망 정비·비상대응 체계를 통해 안정적이고 지속가능한 물 공급 체계를 마련해 나가고 있습니다.

1. 주요 물 공급원
- 창원시는 주로 칠서정수장과 대산정수장을 통해 수돗물을 공급받고 있음.
- 이 두 정수장은 창원시의 주요 수돗물 공급원으로, 정수 처리된 물이 창원시 전역으로 공급됨.
- 물 공급원은 강수, 습지, 강, 호수의 물을 포함한 탁수 표면수에 해당.

2. 연간 인출량
- 칠서정수장: 연간 약 122 메가리터(Ml)
- 대산정수장: 연간 약 122 메가리터(Ml)
- 합계: 연간 약 244 메가리터(Ml) 수준

3. 향후 5~10년 예상 변화
- 기후변화와 산업·인구 수요 증가로 인해 더 많은 양의 인출이 필요할 것으로 예상됨.
- 창원시는 2026년까지 비상연계 공급망 구축사업을 완료할 계획임.
- 칠서정수장과 대산정수장을 연결하여, 비상 상황 시에도 안정적으로 수돗물 공급이 가능하도록 설계.
- 노후 상수관망 정비 및 상수도 시설 현대화 사업도 병행 추진 중.

4. 추가 코멘트
- 창원시는 남강댐과 낙동강 계통이라는 안정적인 수자원 기반 위에, 대산·칠서·석동정수장 등 다중 정수장 운영으로 수원 다변화를 확보하고 있습니다.

Surface water:
Water in our streams, rivers, lakes, reservoirs, dams and wetlands is known as surface water. 
Surface water systems are replenished by rainfall and when groundwater discharges to the 
surface. Surface water from the River Murray and Mount Lofty Ranges is treated to provide 
drinking water for Greater Adelaide. 

River Murray:
Water from the River Murray is treated to provide drinking water for Greater Adelaide and many 
regional towns across South Australia, as well as industrial use and irrigation. The River Murray 
also supports important floodplains, wetlands and ecosystems along the length of the river.

Reservoirs:
Reservoirs throughout the Mount Lofty Ranges catchment area are an important source of 
water for metropolitan Adelaide. As well as catching and storing rainwater that falls across 
from the Adelaide Hills, reservoirs store water pumped from the River Murray to supplement 
Adelaide's water supply. At full capacity, the reservoirs hold a little less than one year's supply for metropolitan Adelaide.

Note in FY2024/25 the City of Adelaide extracted 231,900 kL directly from the Torrens River.

Seawater:
Desalinated seawater is treated to become high quality drinking water by removing salt and 
impurities using a process called reverse osmosis. It is safe to drink and meets the stringent 
standards set by the Australian Drinking Water Guidelines. Desalinated seawater is a climate 
independent water source that contributes to South Australia's water security.

In metropolitan Adelaide, the Adelaide Desalination Plant has been producing drinking water since late 2011.

Recycled water:
Recycled water is water that comes from sewerage systems, stormwater or industrial processes and is treated to a standard that is safe and appropriate for its end use. Recycled water is a key component of sustainable water use. It can be used for a variety of purposes where water treated to drinking standards is not needed and to reduce the demand on freshwater supplies.

Purified recycled water:
Purified recycled water comes from treated wastewater or stormwater that has gone through 
advanced water treatment processes to filter and purify so it's safe to drink and meets the 
required health and safety standards. Using purified recycled water would improve the diversity of our water supply and our climate resilience, contributing to South Australia's water security.

The primary source of drinking water comes from the Biscayne Aquifer, which is replenish by the Everglades, and is located just below the land surface in South Florida. The Biscayne Aquifer is composed of a porous rock with small cracks and holes through which rainwater seeps and fills. Due to sea level rise, the aquifer is vulnerable to saltwater intrusion, threatening contamination of the water supply. To protect its drinking water, the county is restoring canal systems and installing salinity control structures - gates which help separate fresh water and saltwater. Mangrove forests are being restored too, because they help slow the movement of saltwater through canals, keeping the water behind the gates fresher.

O abastecimento de água de Salvador é garantido por um sistema integrado de captação, tratamento e distribuição operado principalmente pela Empresa Baiana de Águas e Saneamento (Embasa). A cidade é atendida por diversas fontes hídricas, sendo a Barragem de Pedra do Cavalo a principal delas, complementada por outros mananciais como os rios Joanes, Ipitanga e Cobre. A estrutura é composta por várias Estações de Tratamento de Água (ETAs), estrategicamente distribuídas para atender às diferentes regiões do município.
A Barragem de Pedra do Cavalo, localizada no rio Paraguaçu, é responsável por cerca de 60% do abastecimento de Salvador, com uma vazão de captação estimada em 7,0 m³/s (ou 7.000 litros por segundo). Essa água é conduzida até a Estação de Tratamento Principal, que atende a maior parte da população da capital e da Região Metropolitana.
Como reforço ao sistema principal, a Represa Joanes II, localizada no rio Joanes, contribui com uma captação de aproximadamente 1,2 m³/s, podendo alcançar até 2,3 m³/s em sua capacidade máxima. Essa água também é direcionada à ETA Principal.
A ETA Suburbana, por sua vez, é abastecida pelas represas Ipitanga I e II, que juntas operam com uma capacidade de tratamento de cerca de 400 litros por segundo, atendendo principalmente à região do Subúrbio Ferroviário de Salvador.
Outra fonte complementar é a Represa do Rio do Cobre, que abastece a ETA Cobre, com capacidade de tratamento de aproximadamente 100 litros por segundo, sendo responsável pelo suprimento de áreas como a Enseada do Cabrito.
Segundo dados mais recentes disponíveis da Embasa, a capacidade total instalada de produção de água tratada em Salvador é de cerca de 16.000 litros por segundo, distribuídos entre as ETAs Principal, Suburbana, Cobre, Vieira de Mello e Teodoro Sampaio. No entanto, o volume efetivamente tratado e distribuído em 2021 foi de aproximadamente 11.181 litros por segundo, o que equivale a cerca de 823 mil metros cúbicos por dia, volume suficiente para atender a uma população urbana de aproximadamente 2,4 milhões de habitantes.
Em resumo:
Barragem de Pedra do Cavalo - 7.000 L/s (~60% do abastecimento);
Represa Joanes II - 1.200 L/s;
Represas Ipitanga I e II - 400 L/s;
Represa do Rio do Cobre - 100 L/s.
Portanto, o sistema de abastecimento de Salvador é robusto e diversificado, com fontes de grande escala e reservatórios complementares que garantem a continuidade e a segurança hídrica da capital baiana.

The jurisdiction's potable water supply is exclusively drawn from the Lower Floridan Aquifer, a deep groundwater source. According to the OUC Water Quality Report (attached), the utility pumps approximately 32.3 billion gallons of water annually for its customers, covering a service area of 200 square miles. This utility serves not only the city of Orlando but also parts of unincorporated Orange County. Therefore, it is essential to estimate the amount of water supplied specifically to the city of Orlando.

Based on data from the United States Census Bureau, Orlando has a land area of 110.6 square miles, which represents about 55% of the total 200-square-mile service area. Consequently, the estimated amount of water supplied exclusively to the city of Orlando is approximately 17.8619 billion gallons per year. This figure is equivalent to 67614.6 megaliters per year.

Looking ahead, a significant volume of water is projected to be withdrawn. The OUC is currently constructing a reverse osmosis treatment facility in Lake Nona to draw water from the Deep Lower Floridan Aquifer. Additionally, OUC is collaborating closely with the Central Florida Water Initiative to explore alternative water supplies and implement stricter conservation measures. These developments will help ensure that total withdrawals remain sustainable, despite anticipated population growth.

A projection conducted by the Central Florida Water Initiative (CFWI) also indicates that demand pressures are increasing (report is attached). The CFWI region, which includes Orange, Osceola, Polk, Seminole, and Southern Lake County, housed approximately 2.9 million people in 2015. This number is projected to reach 4.4 million by 2040. The report also highlights that average daily water use in these regions is expected to rise from 667 million gallons per day in 2015 to 908 million gallons per day by 2040, with groundwater accounting for an increase from 635 million gallons per day to 855 million gallons per day.

column18: The Scioto River begins as a small creek about 80 miles north in Hardin County, northwest of Kenton, Ohio. Rolling through woods and farmlands, this river remains a main water source for Columbus. The Griggs and O'Shaugnessy Reservoirs, located on the Scioto River, along with the Doutt Upground Reservoir (an off stream reservoir), have a combined storage capacity of 14.2 billion gallons, holding only a small percentage of the water that flows through Columbus, and providing water for downtown, west and northwest Franklin County. Family picnics, fishing, boating, and waterskiing in the recreation area surrounding and including both reservoirs are enjoyed by thousands every summer. Big Walnut Creek forms about 20 miles northeast of Columbus and feeds Hoover Reservoir. column18: Effective drinking water management hinges on several key elements: water resource planning, treatment processes, distribution infrastructure, reducing water loss, and preserving water quality. Our institution has been proactively diversifying its drinking water sources by exploring alternative local options. Concurrently, we've implemented numerous administrative and physical measures to curb network losses and optimize water usage. To alleviate the strain on drinking water supplies, we've been investing in and promoting the supply of reclaimed water to industries. As part of our Drought Mitigation Strategy, we've constructed a transmission line connecting the Sapanca Lake and Yuvacık Dam Drinking Water Treatment Plant. This strategic move positions Sapanca Lake as a backup water source. Should the capacity of Yuvacık Dam prove insufficient, the transmission line is activated to safeguard the city's water supply. This investment has been instrumental in averting mandatory water cuts and the need for rotational water supply, which are common during water shortages.

Sources of water supply:
Athienou's water supply is managed within the national water system of Cyprus, which combines desalination, surface water from dams, groundwater abstraction, and limited use of recycled water for irrigation.

Estimated volumes withdrawn (national distribution, applied locally):

Desalination: approx. 60-65% of total supply

Surface water (dams): approx. 20-25%

Groundwater: approx. 10-15%

Recycled water (non-potable, mainly for irrigation): small share

Projected change:

Desalination: expected to increase or remain stable, becoming the dominant source due to increasing drought.

Surface water: expected to decrease in reliability because of reduced rainfall and higher evaporation rates.

Groundwater: projected to decrease due to over-extraction risks and declining water quality.

Recycled water: projected to increase as part of national efforts to expand reuse for agriculture and reduce pressure on potable sources.

El distrito de San Borja cuenta con un servicio de agua potable de alta calidad, gestionado principalmente por la empresa estatal SEDAPAL, que garantiza el abastecimiento continuo y seguro a la mayoría de hogares, instituciones y comercios del distrito. El acceso al agua potable es casi universal, beneficiando a más del 95% de la población, lo que contribuye significativamente a la salud pública y al bienestar de los vecinos.

San Borja ha implementado además programas orientados a la gestión sostenible del recurso hídrico, promoviendo el uso responsable del agua mediante campañas de sensibilización ciudadana y educación ambiental. Estas iniciativas buscan reducir el consumo excesivo y fomentar prácticas de ahorro, como la instalación de dispositivos de bajo consumo y la reparación oportuna de fugas.

El distrito también trabaja en coordinación con organismos técnicos para mantener la infraestructura hidráulica en óptimas condiciones y evitar pérdidas. Asimismo, se desarrollan proyectos para el uso eficiente del agua en áreas verdes públicas, utilizando sistemas de riego tecnificado y captación de aguas pluviales.

En resumen, San Borja garantiza un servicio de agua potable confiable y sostenible, incorporando esfuerzos para conservar el recurso y mejorar la calidad de vida de su población.
